sections.heading: The idea
sections.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
sections.body_md:
The simplex method walks from one basic feasible solution to a neighbor with a better objective, until no neighbor is better. For a minimization, the reduced costs are the slopes of those edges. If every reduced cost is nonnegative, the current basis is optimal: raising any nonbasic variable cannot decrease the cost.

If some reduced cost is negative, that column may enter. The ratio test then looks at the positive entries of the updated column. The smallest ratio names the basic variable that hits zero first, and that variable leaves. The basis changes by exactly one column. If the entering column has no positive entry, no basic variable ever hits zero, the step may be arbitrarily long, and the objective is unbounded below.

Which negative reduced cost enters is a pivot rule. The most negative rule is one choice. Any other negative reduced cost is also a descent step. Different rules can take different paths and different numbers of pivots. The optimality test and the unboundedness test stay the same.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md: At a basis \(B\), the reduced cost of column \(j\) is \(\bar{c}_j = c_j - c_B^T B^{-1} A_j\), and the updated column is \(\bar{a}_j = B^{-1} A_j\). The leaving row minimizes \(\bar{b}_i / \bar{a}_{ij}\) over positive \(\bar{a}_{ij}\). One blocking row with value \(p\) and positive entry \(r\) gives the ratio \(p/r\). After a step \(\theta\), the objective changes by \(\theta \bar{c}_j\). Optimality is \(\bar{c}_j \ge 0\) for every nonbasic \(j\). Unboundedness is some \(\bar{c}_j < 0\) with every entry of \(\bar{a}_j\) nonpositive.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Minimize \(-2x - 5y\) subject to \(x + y + s = 9\) and \(2x + y + t = 12\), from the slack basis. The reduced costs are \(-2\) and \(-5\). Enter \(y\). Its column is \((1, 1)\), and the ratios are 9 and 12, so the step is 9 and \(s\) leaves. The new point is \(y = 9\), \(t = 3\), with objective \(-45\).

The kiln value is -45. The reduced costs of the nonbasic columns at this basis are positive, so the basis is optimal. Entering \(x\) first would have been a legal descent step as well, with a less negative slope. That path is longer and ends at the same value. The optimum is unique.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Stopping because a pivot was made is not the optimality test. The test is the sign of every reduced cost after the pivot. A second miss is to take the larger ratio and drive a basic variable negative. The leaving variable is a minimum-ratio row. A third is to treat one negative reduced cost with an all-nonpositive column as an ordinary pivot. There is no leaving variable, and the program is unbounded below. A fourth is to believe the most-negative rule is the only correct entering choice. It is one rule. Descent only needs some negative reduced cost.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The iteration assumes a basic feasible solution is already in hand. The slack basis supplies one when the right-hand side is nonnegative. When it is not, or when the equalities were built with surpluses, an auxiliary problem with artificial variables either returns a first basis or proves that the original system is empty. That auxiliary problem is itself solved by the iteration just described.
